subject: physics

moments.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa
moments.body: Galileo allegedly drops a cannonball and a musket ball from the top of the Leaning Tower of Pisa. They land at the same time, contradicting Aristotle's claim that heavier objects fall faster. There is no contemporary record; it was reported by Galileo's student Viviani decades later. Galileo certainly did the experiment on inclined planes.
moments.takeaway: Whether or not it happened, the Pisa demonstration captures the death of Aristotelian physics.

moments.title: Inclined plane experiments
moments.body: Galileo rolls bronze balls down polished wooden inclines, measuring distances and times. He finds distance is proportional to time squared — uniform acceleration. He uses his pulse and a water clock for timing.
moments.takeaway: Modern physics begins with patient measurement, not philosophical argument.

moments.title: Two New Sciences
moments.body: Smuggled to a Dutch publisher, Galileo's last book presents his complete mechanics. He shows projectile motion is parabolic — the composition of horizontal motion with vertical acceleration. This is the first textbook of mathematical physics.
moments.takeaway: Under house arrest, Galileo founds modern mechanics.

moments.title: Hammer and feather on the Moon
moments.body: Astronaut Dave Scott drops a geological hammer and a falcon feather on the lunar surface. With no air, they hit the dust simultaneously — Galileo vindicated, 333 years after his death, on another world.
moments.takeaway: Galileo's claim is finally tested in a true vacuum — on the Moon.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The equivalence principle has been tested to 1 part in 10^15 by the MICROSCOPE satellite (2017). Lunar laser ranging tests it for the Earth and Moon falling around the Sun.
now.open_questions: Does the equivalence principle hold for quantum particles?

reflection: Galileo's inclined plane experiments were tedious; the tower story is what we remember. Why do we prefer dramatic myths to slow truth?
